## 1. Direct speech and indirect speech

To report what a person says, one can transcribe the exact words that this person pronounces, introducing them appropriately if need be:

> **Theodoricus dicit** (dicebat, dixit, dicet): **«Frater meus abest»**, *Thierry says (was saying, said, will say): «My brother is not there».*

This is *direct speech*: we have almost always used it in this book, because it better conveys living reality. It is however useful for you to know the other method, called *indirect speech*, for numerous Latin authors (Caesar, Cicero, etc.) use it abundantly.

### 1° What does the simple sentence become in indirect speech?

Let us take the previous example again. We will have:

> **Theodoricus fratrem suum abesse dicit** (dicebat, etc.).

You will notice that the INDEPENDENT clause in the indicative of direct speech becomes a SUBORDINATE INFINITIVE clause in indirect speech.

### 2° What does an interrogative clause become?

Example:

> **Th. dicit: «Ubi est frater meus?».**

It is transformed into a COMPLETIVE clause (cf. Grammatical appendix, § 70) IN THE SUBJUNCTIVE:

> **Th. quaerit ubi sit frater suus**, *Th. asks where his brother is.*

Note that not only have we transformed the pronoun as above (meus into suus), but we have had to replace dicit by quaerit to better mark the INTERROGATION.

### 3° What does a subordinate become in indirect speech?

- if it is in the INDICATIVE, it passes into the SUBJUNCTIVE;
- if it is in the SUBJUNCTIVE or in the INFINITIVE, IT DOES NOT CHANGE mood.

Example:

> **Th. dicit: «Nescio ubi sit frater meus quia eum videre non possum»,**

becomes:

> **Th. dicit se nescire ubi sit frater suus quia eum videre non possit.**

N.B. — Completives that are objects of verbs such as scire, nescire, cogitare, etc., are INDIRECT INTERROGATIVES (and are therefore in the SUBJUNCTIVE) when they are introduced by interrogative words, pronouns or adverbs, such as quis, ubi, etc.

In summary, the INDICATIVE becomes INFINITIVE or SUBJUNCTIVE, while the INFINITIVE and the SUBJUNCTIVE are kept.

## 2. Sequence of tenses in indirect speech

### A) The direct questions

We are going to take as an example an independent clause that we will then introduce into indirect speech.

Let the following direct questions be:

| | Latin | English | |
|---|---|---|---|
| a) | **Quid cras facies?** | *What will you do tomorrow?* | FUTURE |
| b) | **Quid hodie facis?** | *What are you doing today?* | PRESENT |
| c) | **Quid heri faciebas?** | *What were you doing yesterday?* | PAST |
| | **Quid heri fecisti?** | *What did you do yesterday?* | |
| | **Quid heri feceras?** | *What had you done yesterday?* | |

### B) In indirect interrogation (subjunctive)

What will these tenses become in indirect interrogation in the subjunctive? Two cases are to be considered:

**1° The MAIN VERB is in the PRESENT or in the FUTURE**; in other words one reports today (or one will report tomorrow) the terms of the direct interrogations above. We will have for example:

— if we put our question today: **(hodie) quaerimus** (ind. pres.), *(today) we ask:*

| | Latin | Tense | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| a) | **quid cras sis facturus** | subj. pres. of esse + fut. part. | *what you will do tomorrow* |
| b) | **quid hodie facias** | subj. pres. | *what you are doing today* |
| c) | **quid heri feceris** | subj. perf. | *what you did yesterday* |

— if we put our question later: **(cras) quaeremus** (ind. fut.), *(tomorrow) we will ask…*

| | Latin | Tense | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| a) | **quid postero die sis facturus** | subj. pres. of esse + fut. part. | *what you will do the next day* |
| b) | **quid ipso die facias** | subj. pres. | *what you are doing the same day* |
| c) | **quid praeterito die feceris** | subj. perf. | *what you will have done the previous day* |

In summary, if the main verb (here scire) is in the present or in the future (of the INFECTUM), the verb of the subordinate is in the present of the INFECTUM or of the PERFECTUM:

- PRESENT SUBJUNCTIVE (of the infectum) if the subordinate action takes place at the same time as the main action (b);
- PRESENT SUBJUNCTIVE of the auxiliary esse and FUTURE PARTICIPLE if it takes place after (a);
- PERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (that is to say present of the PERFECTUM) if the subordinate action took place before the main action (c).

REMARK. — We have added adverbs of time (hodie, cras, etc.) to better bring out the dates of the actions. One can replace them by others (for example heri instead of hodie in the last example) provided one does not upset the order of the actions. One can also remove them; e.g.: quaeremus quid feceris.

**2° The MAIN VERB is in the PAST.**

**(heri, *yesterday*) quaerebamus** (ind. impf.), *we were asking*; **quaesivimus** (ind. pft), *we asked*; **quaesiveramus** (ind. p.q.p.), *we had asked:*

| | Latin | Tense | English |
|---|---|---|---|
| a) | **quid postero die facturus esses** | subj. impf. of esse + fut. part. | *what you were going to do the next day* |
| b) | **quid ipso die faceres** | subj. impf. | *what you were doing the same day* |
| c) | **quid praeterito die fecisses** | subj. p.q.p. | *what you had done the previous day* |

The verb of the subordinate is in the past of the INFECTUM or of the PERFECTUM:

- IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (that is to say past of the INFECTUM) if the subordinate action takes place at the same time as the main action (b);
- IMPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE of the auxiliary with the future participle if it takes place after (a);
- PLUPERFECT SUBJUNCTIVE (that is to say past of the PERFECTUM) if it took place before (c).

### C) In indirect speech in the infinitive

What will these tenses become in indirect speech in the infinitive?

The infinitive having three tenses, the PRESENT, the PERFECT and the FUTURE, the logic of its use is very simple:

- PRESENT infinitive if the two actions take place at the same time;
- FUTURE infinitive if the subordinate action takes place after;
- PERFECT infinitive if the subordinate action took place before.

Let us report the following words of Vincent:

> **Vincentius dicit** (dicebat, etc.): **«Heri nihil feci, hodie nihil facio, cras nihil faciam».**

We will simply have, for example:

| | Main verb | Before | Same time | After |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Present | **Hodie Vincentius dicit…** | **se heri nihil fecisse** | **se hodie nihil facere** | **se cras nihil facturum esse** |
| Past | **Heri Vincentius dicebat** (dixit, dixerat)… | **se praeterito die nihil fecisse** | **se ipso die nihil facere** | **se postero die nihil facturum esse** |

And, if the main action (dicere) is in the future, it will still be the same thing.

*Conclusion:* You see that the infinitive clause is a remarkably practical tool. Know how to profit from it!

## 3. The choice of moods and tenses in the complex sentence

A complex sentence comprises a main clause (or even several coordinated clauses linked by words such as et, sed, etc.) and subordinate clauses which can be COMPLETIVE (as in the examples above) or not (e.g. adverbial). One must at least know that:

1° In an independent, main or coordinated clause, the mood and the tense of the verb are chosen uniquely according to the sense and the real tenses of the facts one wants to express. It will therefore be enough to apply the indications relating to moods and tenses which are given in the grammatical appendix, §§ 62 to 69.

2° Completive clauses (of which you will find examples in the grammatical appendix §§ 70 and 71) follow the rules of sequence of which we have just given you the essentials in the course of the present revision.

3° Adverbial and relative clauses (cf. grammatical appendix, §§ 72 to 79) constitute an intermediate case. The choice of mood and tense generally depends on the nature of the facts to be expressed. However, certain turns of phrase or certain linking words can dictate this choice. Thus certain SUBORDINATING CONJUNCTIONS are always constructed with the INDICATIVE; others always with the SUBJUNCTIVE; others with one or the other ACCORDING TO THE SENSE. Do not forget that you have in the grammatical appendix a table (§ 49) giving you this information for the principal subordinating conjunctions.

Likewise the verbs which are constructed with completive clauses can require such or such construction. Example:

- jubere is constructed with the infinitive clause: **jubeo te venire**, *I order you to come*,
- whereas imperare is constructed with ut and the subjunctive: **impero ut venias**, *I order that you come*.

If you find this lesson too arduous, content yourself with trying to retain the examples that we have given you in bold type: they will be useful to you.

If on the contrary you think that this setting in order arrives too late, tell yourself that this delay is voluntary: theory presents no interest unless it rests on a solid practice. The first wave had to be essentially practical. In the continuation of the second wave you are not forbidden to put these new pieces of knowledge to good use.

SECOND WAVE: the 49th lesson.
